utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber announced yesterday that it would give a brief statement on the scheduling issue. The Chamber has discussed the matter thoroughly and has found that it needs a bit more time to formulate such a statement. Therefore, the parties will have to wait a little bit longer. That means that we could now continue with the next witness to be called by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only observation I've got so far as that's concerned is the logistical one. We've begun this morning making some efforts to obtain witnesses for the week after next. We will continue doing that. I don't know how fruitful that's proved. I've been involved in other activities. We will continue doing that, Your Honour, but I can only urge the Court, with respect, to inform the parties as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll certainly take care of that and not to allow a situation to happen where you're surprised and that by the silence of the Chamber you'd run into difficulties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then are you ready to call your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that would be Mr. Kasagic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Kasagic, I take it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kasagic. Do you understand -- do you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. [In English] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this Court, Mr. Kasagic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration, of which the text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kasagic. Please be seated. You'll first be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. Mr. Josse, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I'd like to begin, if I may, with a short resume of your career up until this point in time. It's right, isn't it, that you spent most of your career in business, and your last job prior to the political events that you're primarily here to describe was as director of a company called Jelingrad in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Jelsingrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. You had been a member of the League of Communists; however, you were not involved in any particular activity within the League; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kasagic, in fact, you answered that in English. Your English is not terribly good, is it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would be essential for someone in your position, even if their English was good, to answer questions in B/C/S, but I having had the advantage of spoken to you for some time, I'm informing you that you really must answer in B/C/S. Your English isn't anywhere near good enough, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, I think, in order to appreciate every detail of the words you're speaking, you better express yourself in your own language, although it's also appreciated that you took the effort to say a few words in English. But I think that's far better, and the Chamber would prefer you to speak your own language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were also a member of an inspection committee within Banja Luka, and also a judge of the labour court there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Of Bosnia-Herzegovina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And that really takes us to November 1990, when you were elected in the first multi-party elections to the Assembly, or the Parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a moment. You were an SDS candidate. In 1992, the early part of that year, you became the president of the Executive Committee within Banja Luka and you combined that job with being a member of what was then the Serb Assembly within the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. However, I believe that the elections for the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka were held in February 1991, where I was president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's my fault. You remained president of the Executive Committee until December of 1995, when you --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Until the 20th of December, 1995, when I became prime minister of Republika Srpska -- was appointed prime minister of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. And you held that post for just under five months?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Four days short of five months.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Having been dismissed from that job, you were then in fact unemployed for a number of years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I was unemployed for four years; however, I was working on my doctoral studies and involved in scientific research. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You got your doctorate in what subject, please?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Settlement of international commercial disputes through arbitration.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And having got that doctorate, you got a job as a university teacher?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what is your present employment?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Professor at the faculty of economics in Banja Luka and Brcko. I teach business law.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you about an experience that you had in the springtime of 1990 in Croatia, at about the time of the Eurovision Song Contest.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were in Croatia at that time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes, in Pula.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what did you hear on the radio or the television there that caused you concern?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I was listening to Tudjman commenting on why the competition was said to be in Yugoslavia and not in Croatia. All those present were Croats, and I said that when a competition is held in France, then one would say that it is held in France and Paris. However, one never mentions the republic wherein it is held; rather, one mentions the state itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And could you describe how you saw tensions rising as a result of decisions of the constitutional court within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The constitutional court of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the president of which was Mr. Kasim Trnka, examined the applications by parties, or rather, I believe it was by the SDA. It was a proposal by the Muslim side to assess the constitutionality of the establishment of political parties. The constitutional court accepted that the establishment of political -- national political parties was constitutional, and therefore, their establishment was thus confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And so which party was formed first as a result of that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: At the time, the Croatian Democratic Community already existed in Croatia. Subsequently, the SDA was established, in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as a Bosniak party; and the last one to be established was the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I just ask a few clarifying questions on the issue which is the decision. You told us that the president of the constitutional court was Mr. Kasim Trnka. From his name, what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A Muslim, a Bosniak. At the time, he was a Muslim. Now he's a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What was the composition of the constitutional court at that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know that. But the composition was mixed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was mixed. No majority for Bosniaks or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who constituted the majority, but I know that all the organs had to be mixed in terms of ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the vote of the president have any special significance in the constitutional court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in September 1990. The SDS was formed in July 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Why did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The main objective was to get involved in the multi-party system, because all my life I had lived in a single-party system and I wanted to stand once and for all against the communists. And it was only these parties that -- newly established that could stand ground against the communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were there any other viable parties for you to join?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There was the Socialist Party. I talked to some people about this. However, one of the members of the -- or rather, some of the members of the Socialist Party stated that I wasn't suitable to be a member. One of them was a Croat who said so. I myself thought at the time that there was really no difference between the Socialist Party and the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And how was it, as far as you're concerned, that you were selected as an SDS candidate for the November 1990 election?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There were few intellectuals in the Serb Democratic Party. The ones who were intellectuals were nominated for MPs. As far as I remember, all of them had university degrees, masters degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And having been selected, as you've already told us, you were elected in November 1990. And it's right, isn't it, that being a member of the Assembly was not a full-time job? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: It was on a voluntary basis. I was still employed with Jelsingrad, until I was elected the president of the Executive Committee of the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How would you describe initial cooperation between the three main ethnic parties in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: We were fully united against the League of Communists, and it was for the first time that we went along, under a multi-party system. We even cast unanimous votes. However, a rift emerged with the rising of ethnic tensions. The Serbs were against the abolition of Yugoslavia. The Bosniaks and Croats were in favour of Bosnia-Herzegovina's separation from Yugoslavia. We knew that it was anti-constitutional and that only the Parliament of Yugoslavia could decide on such a matter, and not a Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is where the conflict emerged.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe, if you can, in a bit more detail, some of the points of conflict, particularly those that stick out in your mind as being further concern and reasons for the ultimate breakup of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. He said that he -- that Bosnia-Herzegovina was going to remain in Yugoslavia only if Croatia also agreed to do so, while Slovenia would be free to go. There were attempts to keep Bosnia within Yugoslavia along with Serbia, Montenegro, and Macedonia. There were some successful negotiations. Even Muhamed Cengic put it forward as a motion at an Assembly session. However, shortly afterwards, this position was refuted by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic. Serb MPs asked for the establishment of a council for the protection of ethnic interests, in accordance with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was supposed to take a view on this matter. This motion was denied, and the Serb Democratic Party withdrew, or rather, its MPs withdrew, because they did not wish to participate in a referendum for the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The parliament continued operating without the SDS MPs, and a referendum was held in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina leaving Yugoslavia in March 1991. The voting during the referendum was not held under control, but it was concluded that 63 per cent of citizens were in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina leaving Yugoslavia. That was the official information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, I'd like, whilst we're on this part of the evidence, to ask you about Mr. Krajisnik and his role as Speaker of the Assembly. Firstly, did you know Mr. Krajisnik prior to your both being elected as members of that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know him. The first time I saw him was when he was proposed as a candidate for the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That was in Djuro Djakovic [phoen] Street in Sarajevo at the caucus of SDS party members.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is your recollection as to how he came to be selected for that job at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: He became candidate -- actually, it was Milan Trbojevic who was proposed as the candidate for president, but he was not adopted because we thought that nobody from Krajina held any high positions in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We wanted somebody from Krajina to be in that high position, and everybody who is resident of Krajina is Krajisnik, and somebody called Krajisnik at home, he was not at that session. He came, and that's when I saw him for the first time. The then president of the SDS said: Members from Krajina want Krajisnik. That's why we propose Krajisnik as the president of the BiH Assembly. Everybody accepted Krajisnik as the candidate who would later on be selected as the president of the BiH Assembly. He hails from Krajina, and hence his family name, Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Having been duly appointed president of the Assembly, how did you assess his handling of the job?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: After the mono-party system, when the parliament took all of its decisions in advance, without a public debate, he was really doing well at the multi-party Assembly. He gave the floor to everybody who wanted to take it. I perceived him as a legalist, as a person who did not deny anybody's right as MP. All the MPs wanted to say something. This was their first opportunity to say something freely and openly. The Assembly lasted quite a long time, and he was also praised on the ground as the person who chaired the assembly sessions really well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What, if anything, was Mr. Krajisnik's influence within the SDS Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: He was the first among the equals. He was just one among the MPs. The other MPs did not allow anybody to influence their opinion. I even said once: Nobody's going to deny me the right to my intellectual thought. And the rest of us were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What would you say to the proposition that Mr. Krajisnik had his own clique of deputies, in effect, his own Deputies Club within the parliament?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: He couldn't have this. As MPs, we were given some rights and freedoms and we worked as brothers. We were all very good friends. There were no need for anybody to stand out in this club.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think you've already described the breakup of the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament and the formation of the Serb parliament. Do you remember when that took place?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Before the war, in early 1992. The HDZ MPs wanted to have a referendum on secession of Bosnia, and they did not want to adopt our proposal that we should have a Council for National Security established in order to review that desire. This council would have been composed of members of the three peoples and members of other nationalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you've told us that by early 1991, you had become the president of the Executive Committee in Banja Luka, which was a full-time job. You're nodding, so that's obviously right. Perhaps you could go on, give us some approximation --

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- as to how much of your time thereafter was spent on Banja Luka municipal affairs as against republican affairs in your capacity as a member of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: As president of the Municipal Board, I didn't have working hours. I worked all the time. I gave this job over a hundred per cent. However, if we said that the working hours were a hundred per cent of the time, I could then say that my work in the parliament accounted for 5 per cent of my working hours and my work in the municipality for 95 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I should ask you one other thing before we turn to Banja Luka. As time went on, before the war I'm talking about, how did your relationship with Mr. Krajisnik develop? In other words, how did you get on with him on a personal level?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There was no difference between me and Mr. Krajisnik as opposed to other MPs. We had a business relationship and a friendly relationship. There were no particular arrangements between the two of us as regards any matter that we had to deal with. We were not even family friends. I know that he has three children. At that time, his wife was alive. And he knows that I have a wife and two children. However, our families never met.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik show respect to Muslim members of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: As the president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he respected everybody the same, across the board. Two or three days ago, as I was leaving to come here, a Bosniak from Brcko asked me to give him his regards because he has a high opinion of Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik allow members of other ethnic groups to, for example, practice their religions; and if so, how did he show that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is a religious person himself, and he respects his own religion as much as he respects other people's religion, because he believes that you cannot be a religious person without respecting other people's religion. He allowed Muslim members of the Assembly to have a break during the Ramadan, during their biggest religious holiday, and whenever they asked for a break in order to participate in their religious services, he would allow them that. He did not even want to hear anybody else's opinion as to whether they are entitled to that or not. He would just break and give them time to participate in their religious services.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What is your recollection of SDA demands for dual citizenship of ex-Yugoslav citizens who had gone to live in Turkey sometime during the course of the twentieth century?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: They said that the second and third generation of Bosniaks, including about two or three million of them living in Turkey, and they wanted dual citizenship in order to allow those people to be members of Bosnia and Herzegovina, although they had even moved out from different republics of ex-Yugoslavia. A law on dual citizenship should have been adopted by the Assembly, and if that had taken place, they would have had three million votes more, or even more than that, depending on how many people of age fell under that condition at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And to your recollection, how seriously was this being advocated by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Only the SDA asked for the law on dual citizenship, and this was put on the agenda of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, in the meantime, a referendum on the secession of Bosnia took place. The other parties never asked for such a law to be passed. The SDA was the only party that wanted that to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That doesn't quite answer my question, Mr. Kasagic. To your mind, at the time, how seriously do you think the SDA were advocating this?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: That law would have been passed, and dual citizenship could have been granted to the Serbs who had moved out from Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the Croats who had moved out to Croatia. However, they were a minority with regard to those who had moved out to Turkey. We didn't oppose that, although we were clear that we would have become a minority and that the SDA would have been able to rule based on those votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Banja Luka municipality was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could I just ask one question to clarify the last answer. As a matter of fact, two smaller questions. You said dual citizenship could have been granted to the Serbs who had moved out from Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you continued by saying, "to the Croats who had moved out to Croatia." May I take it from Bosnia and Herzegovina to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Bosnia-Herzegovina to Croatia, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the last part of your answer reads: "We didn't oppose that, although we were clear that we would have become a minority and that the SDA would have been able to rule based on those votes." You say you didn't oppose it. Was that the SDS? Because from what I understand, SDA and SDS, if they would have shared their view on that, this was not something to oppose to, why was it then not adopted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SDS MPs did not oppose that. However, the programme of the work of the Assembly contained the proposal to adopt this law. This programme was never carried through because of the referendum on the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia, and as a result of that, the establishment of a new Assembly, the Assembly of Republika Srpska. In other words, the war started and prevented that law from being adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, then I might have had some difficulties in understanding your question and what you're trying to establish. I do understand from the witness that the SDS did not oppose, and you asked how serious they were. Well, they may have been very serious, but the SDS did not oppose. I mean, what do I have to understand the point to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would be a comment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll -- that's the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's not -- yes. I'm not inviting for your comments. But if I had some misunderstanding, if it would have become clear to you that I misunderstood either the question or the answer, then of course I'd like you to assist me. But if not, then we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps I will deal with it like this with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did this proposition from the SDA add in any way to the ethnic tensions that you've described?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: A lot of things before that contributed to the tensions, and the media played a big role in that. But the politicians also. Izetbegovic wanted to separate Bosnia and Herzegovina from the rest of Yugoslavia at any cost. At the parliament he even stated that he would sacrifice freedom for a sovereign Bosnia. There were a lot of minor things that contributed to the rise of tensions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just try to find out -- we have heard this quote several times, but then it was always sacrifice peace for sovereignty. Is this -- are we talking about the same -- perhaps I should ask the witness. We heard this quote several times, but then it was "peace for sovereignty" rather than "freedom for sovereignty."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was peace, yes, peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me go back to this issue of the individuals in Turkey who were potentially being offered dual citizenship. You've told us that the SDS were not actually opposing the plan, but my question was: Did the plan of the SDA in relation to these citizens in any way affect ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but if I've been following the questions and answers accurately, we're not -- I think the question slightly mischaracterises the nature of the parliamentary proposal and the evidence given by the witness. I don't understand it to be a plan directed toward people in Turkey. It's a proposal for dual citizenship, as the witness related. And I don't think a question should transform that parliamentary proposal into something which it was not and then ask the witness to answer a question about a proposal that was not in fact before the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I just briefly say a few words about that. Of course, what was a project of -- that's at least how I understood the testimony of the witness, which was a project on legislation on dual citizenship, became an issue of dual citizenship for what the witness called a majority, because he was talking about that those who left for Turkey were in a majority compared to the ones who left to Croatia and the ones -- and the Serbs who had left. So to that extent, the issue was a double one: Project for legislation; at the same time, a realistic problem that seemed to arise from that. But there's another matter. The question has been answered to the extent that the witness explained to us that what happened before that added to the tensions. But let's see. When you answered the question by Mr. Josse whether it added to the ethnic tension, you told us what added to the tension before. Would you tell us in what way this, as far as I understand, not at the level of MPs contested issue further added to the ethnic tensions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think this had a significant contribution, because this was not made public. The general public was not aware of this proposal. Among the people, there were other things, like projects of settling Muslims in some parts of Krajina, some other projects according to which they would rule Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answer is clear. The first part of the answer is most relevant to the question. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That does clarify the matter, and I'm certainly not going to return to that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But you were beginning to tell the Chamber about matters that were of more concern to the public and matters that the public viewed as perhaps causing tensions, and you were telling us about the settling of Muslims in some parts of Krajina. Go on, please, with any other examples that you can give.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: That was not settling as such. It was a project. I don't know whether it was a rumour or not. It was said that they would settle around Banja Luka, in one part of Krajina. Throughout the existence of Yugoslavia, they settled in Sandzak and mostly in Sarajevo, and to a lesser extent in Banja Luka. But that was part of normal movement of people in the former Yugoslavia. Most of the Serbs settled in Belgrade and a majority of Croats settled in Zagreb. That was only normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Well, I'm now going to ask you a number of questions about the Banja Luka municipality. You lived there throughout the whole of this period; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It was controlled by the SDS after the elections there?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was there any form of inter-ethnic agreements within Banja Luka, notwithstanding the fact that the SDS were the largest party?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The government was established based on the agreement between the national parties, the SDS, the SDA, and the HDZ. That's how people were selected to the Executive Board. The vice-president of the Municipal Assembly was a Muslim and the deputy chief of police of the region of Banja Luka was also a Muslim. After that inter-party agreement, we managed to establish our municipal government. In the Executive Board, there were two Croats, and as far as I can remember, one Bosniak. I'm sure that there was one. There may have been even more. But I can't remember. The rest were Serbs. One Croat moved out to Rijeka, in Croatia, and the other Croat stayed in the Executive Board throughout the war. The Bosniak also moved out from Banja Luka when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You have said you became president of the Executive Committee in early 1991. How come there was a change of president at that time?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There were elections for MPs in the Municipal Assembly on the same day when the elections for the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina took place. That was in November of the previous year. The parties negotiated power-sharing in the municipality and that had taken some time. After the agreement was reached, the first multi-party government in the municipality of Banja Luka was established on the 8th of February, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Who was president of the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Predrag Radic, a member of the SDS. One of the deputies was either a Serb or a Montenegrin. I don't know how he declared himself. And the other was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you say "one of the deputies," do you mean deputies to the Republican Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to the deputies of the president of the Municipal Assembly. One was a Bosniak and the other was either a Serb or a Montenegrin, which means that he may have hailed from Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean the vice-president?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like you to describe some of the ethnic tensions that had begun to emerge in 1991 within Banja Luka itself. First, perhaps, you could deal with any geographical influence of being near Croatia, or the fact that the municipality was near Croatia, perhaps I should say.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The war broke out in Croatia before that, and it was waged by the Yugoslav People's Army for the preservation of Yugoslavia. Many residents of Krajina were mobilised to go into the war in Croatia. Many of them returned dead, and there were many -- certificates everywhere to be seen. And when a truce was signed with the Croats, this was really a great cause of joy. However, the division along the ethnic lines had already started. The Bosniaks had already formed then their own Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. Members of these parties who had already formed their own assembly went out into the streets, protesting, entering the Municipal Assembly building, and taking the names of those members of the Executive Board who were of Serb ethnicity off the notice boards there. This included my own name, which was taken off -- that is, the plaque was taken off from the door to my office. This was something that was reported by the media. The public at large was aware of this. And this put a stop to these demonstrations or protests. The Municipal Assembly of the Bosniak people never really started functioning. Although no criticism was levelled at their establishment of the Bosniak Municipal Assembly, nor did it cause any conflicts. However, the situation was such that two municipal assemblies were in fact formed in Banja Luka, one of them legal and the other one illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know why there was an attempt to form a Bosniak Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There were such attempts throughout Bosnia, and there were differences of opinions along these ethnic-related matters, tensions heightened, and differences increased. However, I cannot really name a specific cause or reason for that. I don't recall any such reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you say that there were two municipal assemblies, one of them legal, one of them illegal. Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The elections were held on either the 13th or the 15th of November, 1991, for the members of the Municipal Assembly. This was the legal authority. Later on, the Bosniak Municipal Assembly was established in an illegal fashion, without any elections whatsoever. There was one meeting for citizens in general in a sports gymnasium where a decision to this effect was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you. I'd like to know how many members were in that Municipal Assembly, in the legal Municipal Assembly. How many members were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean how many deputies, members? Around 70. I don't know the exact number, whether it was 67 or 70 something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was the ethnic make-up of this assembly, the ethnic make-up in proportion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you any percentages. All the three ethnicities were represented, but Serbs were in the majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the majority, do you have an idea, I'm sure, about the majority. Please, you know, do your best. Recollect, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that the Serb members were able to reach absolute majority, which means that they had over 50 per cent of the votes, or at least around 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Mr. Josse asked you why suddenly there were tensions that had appeared, you answered something like there were tensions everywhere in Bosnia. But I would like you to focus on this municipality that we're interested in, and I'd like you to tell us how these tensions appeared, how, in what shape. Were there special incidents that occurred? Could you please answer us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were no incidents. Tensions were on the increase, and they were coming from outside, as well as locally. There were women protesting in Banja Luka in front of the JNA building against their sons being members of the JNA and exposed to danger. They protested against them waging a war in Croatia. Then women of Serb ethnicity organised counter-demonstrations, chasing away those other women in front of the JNA building, and that was the only open conflict that ever took place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you say, then, that the Banja Luka Assembly, as it was made up, respected the expression of each ethnic group, or was there a trend, like sometimes happens, you know, a trend that the Serbian majority would sort of smother those who didn't have the majority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was the tendency for the establishment of the Association of Municipalities of Banja Luka and other surrounding municipalities, an idea which the other ethnicities opposed. I was the one who presented this idea at the Municipal Assembly session, showing that everything had been done in line with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, there was general distrust and the others opposed the idea. They were outvoted, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Two small clarifying questions as well. On the one hand, you say there were new municipal assemblies, and at the same time you say that -- well, should I say the Muslim -- or the SDA-invented illegal assembly never really came into existence. Did they ever meet, that assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing I saw was that there was this large rally of people in a sports gymnasium, and I saw it on TV. I don't know whether there were any sessions held. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question is: You said, I don't know why they established that. Did it ever come into your mind that where the Municipal Assembly, the legal one, as you said, had an absolute majority of Serbs, that people might fear that their voice was insufficiently heard and that therefore they considered to establish their own platform or their own assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. One could come to that conclusion. But this was true for all the parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a legalist, I simply did not consider anything that was illegal to be serious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you -- from your answer now, I take it that you understood why they did it, but that for legal reasons you considered it not to be taken seriously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said you're a legalist. Does this mean to say that any assembly that has been created which does not find its proper basis in legislation enacted within the Republic, well, to say more or less a shadow assembly, you'd consider that to be an illegal act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unless one opposes unlawfulness, unlawfulness will reign. If there is an illegal assembly that wants to counter another illegal assembly that what we have is simply a general unlawful situation, heightening of tensions, and a situation as it indeed existed at the time in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I have to take this as a yes or as a no? I tend to understand your answer to be that you consider that to be an illegal act, because otherwise these unlawfully created assemblies would challenge the authority or the legal standing of what you consider to be the legal assemblies. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Banja Luka Municipal Assembly acted in full compliance of the law, and I don't believe that there was any need for another assembly to be established illegally. And we should not confuse this with the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which wanted unlawfully to hold a referendum, an idea which was opposed by the SDS MPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it depends on the need and on your judgement of the activities of the legal assembly, whether it is legal or not, to create a counter-assembly; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was telling you about Banja Luka. However, on the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there I was an MP, and I struggled for legality as far as I could, with one vote that I had. Nobody ever opposed the establishment and the operation of the SDA Assembly in Banja Luka. However, it never really operated. I don't know why. Probably they did not have conditions in place for that. Because everything had been done according to law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused. Your last part says: "Because everything had been done according to the law." Everything done by the legal Municipal Assembly, or what did you have in mind when you said "everything"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the legal Assembly, yes. By the legal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Still I have to establish that you've not unequivocally answered my question on whether you consider the creation of a body which is not provided for by law an illegal act; yes or no? Such a body with the same name but then related to a certain ethnicity only.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is a rule of law, then this is the case. If there is no rule of law, then everything is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you the question in a different way. If there would be a municipality in which the Croats would have an absolute majority and where the Serbs would very much feel outvoted, without proper consideration, be taken of their interests. If they would then create a Serb assembly instead of staying within the Assembly established by the law, which had an absolute Croat majority, would you consider that to be an illegal act or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would consider it illegal, just as was the case in Banja Luka. There were no elections held, no MPs were elected, no bodies were elected. It had all been done at this one meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't include that in my question, as a matter of fact. If, well, let's say --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me. I'm going to interrupt for this reason. As a result of these questions, at the moment I'm going to explore the basis for this witness being a legalist, but Your Honour is asking him hypothetical questions. He's based, as far as I can gather, his two assessments on the two bodies hitherto on the actual constitutional framework, one within the municipality, the other within the Republican government. In short, my submission is one can't hypothesise about such things. It's simply not possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can, as a matter of fact. If you consider an existing situation as one on which you could apply legal rules to come to a conclusion whether it's legal or not, then that can be done on a situation which might not actually exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber feels no need to further argue whether one could or not, and leaves the matter as it is. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you, Mr. Kasagic, on what basis -- and I don't mean this rudely, but I think we should explore it -- you call yourself a legalist.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I have a degree in law, I received my doctoral degree, and I teach law, and I believe that the rule of law is the basis of societal order. If there is no rule of law, then we will have the situation as we had in Yugoslavia. Six months before the outbreak of the war, I said that there was no state in place -- there was no state in the world with such a legal system as had existed in Yugoslavia, which was so fragile. A state in the absence of the rule of law ends up in a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've dealt at some length with why you believed the Banja Luka Bosniak Municipal Assembly was illegal. You've only touched on the issue of the Assembly of the Serb People within the Republika Srpska. You've said that you did not believe that to be illegal. Perhaps you'd explain why that is.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: It would not have existed in a country which had a rule of law, because there will only be the Municipal Assembly elected by the people. However, this was in violation of the constitution. The establishment of the council for the protection of ethnic interests was opposed to. They were in favour of holding a referendum, and the Serb MPs established their own assembly in order to protect the constitution of Yugoslavia. Under the Yugoslav constitution, treason was the gravest crime, and the referendum could only be called by Yugoslavia. We were adhering to the Yugoslav constitution, whereas the Bosniak side went even as far as to violate the BiH constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Speaking for yourself, as a Serb and indeed SDS member of the BiH Assembly, why did you feel it necessary to create a Serbian Assembly and thereby, effectively, leave the Assembly to which you had been elected originally? So my question is: Why did you feel it necessary rather than legal?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The only reason was to preserve the state of Yugoslavia and to preserve the constitution. If something had to be changed, then it had to be changed in accordance with the constitution. The breakup of such a state can also have great adverse consequences for the country's economy, which in fact it did. I would never have been opposed had the Yugoslav parliament called the referendum, because this would have been in accordance with the constitution. However, I will always be opposed to anyone who chooses to violate a constitution, including the constitution of our own republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was it possible to change the constitution?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina was frequently amended. Everything was open to amendments. However, I believe that the Serbs were afraid of the possibility that they would be taken out of Yugoslavia. They wanted to remain within that state because it had ensured the quality of all citizens, of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move back, Your Honour, to Banja Luka and some of the ethnic tensions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to ask you, in particular, about 1992 and the tensions immediately before the war. Firstly, you've already mentioned how the Croatian war had affected things a year earlier. Were they affecting things in 1992; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: One could feel the tensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina already at the time of the war in Croatia, because the Bosniaks and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina agreed with the Croatia secession from Yugoslavia, whereas the Serbs opposed it. When the Yugoslav People's Army moved from one place to another, or when it was withdrawing from Slovenia and Croatia, then the women of Bosniak or Croat ethnicities went out into the streets to block the passage of these military convoys. In this way, the army was trapped. The Serbs could not comprehend this, that someone could stop the army, and this caused the tensions. Then, at a session of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we saw women of other ethnicities, I mean of Bosniak and Croat ethnicity, entering the Assembly building and lamenting their sons who were participating in the war in Croatia. Some of them said that their sons had been killed. They were opposed to the Yugoslav People's Army, as such. One of the MPs then spoke out and said that a woman there did not even have a son, and she pretended to be mourning the death of her son. These are just some of the things that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Specifically, was any -- were there any concerns as a result of a decision by Mr. Tudjman to change -- to make a new appointment in relation to a policeman in the southern part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There were national tensions in place. Mr. Tudjman believed that all the policemen were Serbs. There was a football game in 1992 between Dinamo and Crvena Zvezda in Belgrade. There were Serbian supporters from Belgrade. There was fighting between the supporters of Dinamo and the supporters of Crvena Zvezda. The Croatian police officers tried to prevent the fully blown fight between these two groups. They even used force against the Dinamo supporters who were charging against the Serbian supporters. Mr. Tudjman removed those police officers from their positions and he appointed new sets of policemen of Croatian ethnicity. And this was another cause of tensions among the people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I'm looking at the clock. I don't know whether this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It would.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll adjourn until ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I did understand that you wanted to address the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm making very good progress with this witness. The position is that I actually suspect I will only be about half an hour longer. However, at that point, I would appreciate a short break, which effectively would be the last -- partly to speak to Mr. Krajisnik, partly -- there is one other issue. This man was interviewed some years ago by the Office of the Prosecutor, and the Prosecution have been very cooperative, and the interview, in part I have seen but not in whole, it's been looked at by someone on my behalf. I would like the results of that inquiry before I complete my examination-in-chief. So perhaps I could ask for a break whenever I get to the end of my present set of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Sounds very sensible. So you'll be allowed to have a break at that moment for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Kasagic, Mr. Josse will continue his examination. You may proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I next want to ask you, Mr. Kasagic, about some of the work of the Executive Committee, both before and during the war. First the finances, please. How did the municipality manage to stay financially afloat?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: This was provided for by the law. Some of the funds obtained from the taxes was paid into the budget of the Municipal Assembly. During the war, the rate of inflation was 65 per cent a day. The Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka adopted German marks as the means of payment of taxes only. The German marks were valid. The rest were just paper. That's how we stopped the inflation, and Banja Luka had enough funds. All the citizens voluntarily paid their taxes and other contributions in German marks, because the German mark was the only valid means of payment at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What sort of services did the municipality fund?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Communal activities were funded from the municipality. The education was at the level of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Republika Srpska; the judiciary as well. During the war, since this was all interrupted, the funds that we had were used to help financing elementary and secondary education. Also, we had problems with heating and we therefore purchased wood, although there was some oil for some of the facilities in the municipality, namely, the hospital, the Municipal Assembly building, and several schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about sports facilities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: They were also funded from the Municipal Assembly budget. A lot more was allocated for the sports than was in Republika Srpska as a whole. And during the war, the sports were well developed. We funded the maintenance of sports facilities and the sports teams. There were a lot of competitions. There was an international chess competition. There was an international competition in swimming. The teams came to play against our teams. They came from Serbia, from Yugoslavia, and the sports activities were rather well developed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Funds from the Yugoslav National Bank, how were they channelled to your municipality? Or to put it another way, were they channelled via Sarajevo to your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The Central Bank, the National Bank, was in Belgrade. The money that it issued was transferred to the municipalities via the Bank of Bosnia. Before the war started, the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina interrupted cash flows with Banja Luka. I don't know whether it was interrupted with other parts as well. And the cash flows of Yugoslavia were also interrupted, so we were left without any means of financing. From the municipality of Banja Luka, we took a helicopter and flew to Belgrade, to the National Bank of Yugoslavia, and we established cash flows with Gradiska. There was the SDK of Gradiska, that had a connection with the National Bank of Yugoslavia, and through the SDK branch office in Nova Gradiska, we were able to establish cash flows again.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know why the cash flow from the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina was interrupted?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Well, there was just a financial blockade of some parts. The financial cash flows were just interrupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know who was responsible for that financial blockade?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Rumours had it that it was Mr. Izetbegovic who had ordered that, but it was just rumours. I don't have any proof for that. I can't confirm that this was indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The rumours came to you via what source, please?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. It was a long time ago. It was almost 15 years ago. Those were just stories, rumours. There was nothing in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And do you remember how it was that the municipality discovered that these funds had in fact been interrupted, the funds via the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There was no cash flow from the National Bank of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Nothing was coming our way. And we were left without any financing. That's how we noticed. There was no money.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's an obvious question, and to some extent you've just answered it, but perhaps I should just ask it all the same. What effect did it have on the municipality being left without any money?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Nothing special. We managed to resolve that whole situation with the National Bank in Belgrade. We couldn't do anything about the funds in Zagreb, but we established contacts with the National Bank in Belgrade rather quickly. And we were only lucky that the National Bank was not in Zagreb but in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic I'd like to ask you about is refugees, please. Firstly, when did refugees start arriving within your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The first refugees came in 1990. The first refugee was a Serb from Dalmatia, with nine children. I knew his name, but I have forgotten it in the meantime. We provided him with some temporary accommodation. He spent quite a lot of time in Banja Luka, and I don't know where he went next. And then there was a mass exodus of the Serbs from Slavonia, and there were quite a lot of them in the sports hall, Borik, in the sports hall of all the schools. Everything was full of refugees. Some stayed longer, some stayed shorter. Some went to Serbia. The sports halls were gradually becoming empty, but at one moment all the sports halls were full of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was that? When was the sports hall full of refugees? In other words, when was the high point of your refugee problem?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia started in 1990. All the Serbs moved out from Slavonia and moved into Banja Luka, and from Banja Luka they went to other places. I believe that this was in December. I know that it was very cold. If not December, then November. They came on tractors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, may I? You were asked: When was the high point? Then you described when the war started in Croatia and how people moved. Do I have to understand this: That in 1990, you experienced the high point of the refugee problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's when the war started in Croatia. I don't know whether it was in 1990 or 1991, but this was the first in a series of peaks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was not when it started but when it was the high point. So would you please very much concentrate on the questions and try to answer them. So when was the high point? When was it worst?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When Serbian Krajina and the western part of Republika Srpska fell was the time of mass exodus, and I believe that there were some 200 to 300.000 refugees in a column that started at Drvar or Knin and went all the way to Bijeljina. People died and were born by the road. That was the most difficult situation. The roads were absolutely full of people moving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... date that in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1995, I believe, the first half of 1995. It was in July, when Krajina fell in Croatia, and sometime after that, the western part of Republika Srpska fell. I apologise. Yes, yes, it was in 1995, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I just want to be clear about this, Mr. Kasagic: When was it, if you can remember, that the sports hall was full?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: It was full either in 1990 or 1991, when there was the war going on in Croatia. I don't know which year it was, but I know it was cold. It was either late autumn or the beginning of winter of that year. It was very cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the municipality have any problems with refugees from any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: At that time, it only had about 70.000 Serb refugees in Banja Luka. We provided them with accommodation in the sports halls. There were no other refugees at the time. Throughout all the time, most, if not all, the refugees in Banja Luka were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you about population movements in 1992. Firstly, did Muslims leave their homes in Banja Luka in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: When the war in Croatia started, there were no problems in Banja Luka. And when the war started in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there was gradual movement of people. People started moving out, and I don't know how many of them left their homes. I only know that at one point in time the Executive Board decided to give the temporary abandoned houses to other people. That's how these houses and apartments were protected and saved. Whatever was not given for temporary accommodation ended up being completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll come to the subject of temporary abandoned houses in a moment, if I may. But so far as people actually leaving their homes is concerned, was that something which was clearly happening within your municipality?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. When the war started, Serbs, Croats, and Muslims alike were fleeing the war. Some of the Serbs left, and they mostly moved to Serbia. Bosniaks moved to Sweden and the States and Croats moved to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's deal with each of the three groups in turn. Are you able to say why Serbs left Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Those who did not want to participate in the war, the deserters, or at least that's how people treated them, those who did not want to defend their states were considered deserters. But in any case, they were afraid of the war, and that's why they left. One Montenegrin was so afraid of the war that he left for Montenegro and he left his apartment, never to go back to it. The only reason is that they didn't want to participate in the war, they were afraid of the war. They went where it was safe. In Banja Luka, there were periods of when we didn't have electricity for 42 days. It's very difficult to live without electricity. You couldn't clean your apartment, you couldn't do the laundry. If you wanted to have a wash, you had to heat water on the stove. And there was not enough fuel wood for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were any of these Serbs forced from their homes, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No, they were not forced. They were simply fleeing the war. It was a force majeure. That's a situation in which reason prevailed. They were afraid of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll next turn, if I may, to Croats. Why did they leave Banja Luka, as far as you were concerned?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: They lost their jobs. The level of production went down. The rate of employment went down. I don't know whether there were any telephone threats or not, although during the war there were some groups which evicted other ethnic groups from their flats. Those were armed people and directors of companies sought protection from those people. I personally called the director of Jelsingrad, the director of Incel, I called a member of the SDS, asking them to protect the helpless people from those armed groups. There was no protection against them. In any case, they should have been under the jurisdiction of the enforcement agencies and the judiciary. In any case, I called the directors of the companies that owned those apartments, asking them to try and protect their tenants from the armed groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek one clarification, Mr. Josse. You said: "Although during the war there were some groups which evicted other ethnic groups from their flats." Do I have to understand that there were Croatian groups who would evict Serbs and Muslims, and Muslim groups that would evict Serbs and Croats, or could you be a bit more specific on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs evicted Croats and Muslims. I know that a colleague of mine, the president of the Executive Board, sent her husband to protect her colleague and to live with her in her flat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to break down the answer that the witness has just given, because clearly it contains a lot of information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Perhaps before I do that, continue with what you were just saying, Mr. Kasagic, that you know that a colleague of yours, the president of the Executive Board, sent her husband to protect her colleague. Is there anything more you can say about that?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The two of them were both members of the handball team Borac and they were very good friends, and the first one wanted to help the Bosniak colleague. So she sent her husband to share the flat with a colleague for a few nights. However, at the end of that day she left and she lived abroad for a few years. She returned to Banja Luka after the war and now she works at the school of economics. She is my colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The answer you gave a few moments ago was in response to a question that I had asked you about -- specifically about Croats. But the answer where you begun that they lost their jobs and you went on to say that you sought help from directors of companies, including Jelsingrad, presumably referred to Bosniaks as well as Croats; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I was referring to Bosniaks and Croats, so seeking protection for them against eviction. I called the director of Incel Lazo Tomic. I also called Dragan Batar, a member of the SDS, asking them to protect those people from eviction. Banjac told me that this was done by armed people and that this could not be prevented. It took strong police force to stand up against those people and also it took judiciary and the prosecutor's office to bring charges against those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were president of the Executive Committee. Why were you unable to control the situation?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Committee has executive power. He does not have a judiciary power. There were also some secretaries of secretariats who were in charge of communal jobs in the town. There was nobody to look after the security. It was the police's job. And the judiciary was also independent in their dealings. None of these bodies were under the authority of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did the Executive Committee have any control over the police whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness come closer to the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Kasagic, if you could come a little closer to the microphone when you're answering your questions. The interpreters are having a little difficulty hearing you. What about the judiciary? You told us earlier that the municipality funded the judiciary. Bearing that in mind, why didn't the municipality have some control over the judiciary?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The municipality did not fund the judiciary. It just helped with the provision of fuel. It did not fund education. It only contributed to the funding of education during the war. All of that should have been funded from the Republican budget. The judiciary is separated from the executive power. I had executive power within the municipality, and the municipality is tasked with the running of the town, with utility services. We funded sports because we believed that it helped in the development of the young people of our town.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of the things that you were describing, perhaps I could ask you this: Were you aware of forced evictions?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it with my two eyes, but I heard, and a group of Croats came to me, asking protection. This was beyond the scope of my authority, and I couldn't do anything. This was within the authority and of the judiciary. They should have lodged a complaint for trespassing within a month. All those who had been evicted should have done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of, for example, these forced evictions, in your estimation, was there a difference in the treatment meted out by Serbs to Croats and Muslims? In other words, was there any difference between Croats and Muslims in this regard?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: In Banja Luka, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say with any precision, but I believe that it was mostly Muslims and Croats who were evicted. The Serbs were not evicted because they were all on the front line. However, some fighters from the villages wanted to move into town. They even settled the widows of fallen soldiers in the town, and when they moved in, when they settled, they became the subject of social benefits. Dragan Batar, who was a famous boxer before the war, told me that the same thing happened to the Serbs at the hands of Croats and Muslims. I told him that this was not my concern, that I wanted the situation to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as these forced evictions were concerned, who on the Serb side, as far as you know, was responsible for these activities? In other words, who was carrying out these activities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I was told that it was a group of armed people, but nobody ever named any names.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the politics of the region is concerned, did you hold anyone responsible for what was going on?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I was not able to know anything at all about it, because I was not given any names, ever. Those were armed people from companies. Now, who evicted people from flats owned by the municipality, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What happened to the properties that became vacant?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: People would be put up into flats against the law. The Executive Committee would assign some people to flats under a regular procedure and make sure that these people are not evicted. As far as private property is concerned, refugees were temporarily assigned to these properties and they protected them from being damaged and looted. I know that there was a man who referred to my name when he wanted to evict a lady, a Muslim lady, who was a lawyer, and she lived in a flat in the centre of town. Luckily, she was an intelligent woman. She came to me, asking me what it was all about. This man had apparently told her that it had all been agreed with me. I told him that a vacant property is private property and it cannot belong to the state or the municipality, but the municipality would take care of it. However, the lady then went to bring a lawsuit, and this was all settled through court proceedings. Then there were Serbs who came to Banja Luka and evicted a Croat family and took them all the way over to Slavonia, to Okucani, in Croatia. I didn't know anything about this. Only at the point when he realised in Gradiska that he was unable to get them across the border, he brought them back and then asked me what he was going to do about them. I told him: You should take them back to their homes. He told me that they were unable to return home because Serbs from Okucani had been accommodated in their properties. I called the manager of the Bosna Hotel to put up these people in the hotel and that the Executive Committee was to cover the costs for lodging and board. They stayed there some five to seven days, I'm not sure exactly how long, until I heard on Croatian TV that Rajko Kasagic had turned Bosna Hotel into a camp. I called the manager of Bosna Hotel, that he should immediately dissolve the camp, because I had no right to establish or put anyone in any sort of camps. However, in the meantime, the tensions settled down, and I mean the tensions caused by the Serbs who had been driven away from Slavonia into Bosnia. The people who evicted residents from their homes and sent them over to Okucani apparently, so I heard, referred to my name in doing so. I was appointed to a commission which was to assist these Serbs. When I heard them invoking my name whilst evicting people from their homes, I called -- placed a call to the president of Republika Srpska, asking that the commission be abolished because I would no longer do the job as various people were basically ruining my repute. And that night, on TV, I learnt that the commission was indeed dissolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned at the start of the answer that you've just given that refugees were temporarily assigned to vacant properties, as this protected them from being damaged and looted.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: How might these properties be damaged and looted?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Most of the police force was away on the front, and there was no way of protecting properties from looting. If you read Sven Hassel's novels you'll see there was a lot of looting going on in the Balkans during wars. Nobody protected vacant properties. They were looted. Even the windows complete with the frames were taken off. The Yugoslav People's Army, or rather, the air force, asked to be assigned vacant properties in the neighbourhood of Vrbanja, in Banja Luka. They toured all these properties and listed them. The Executive Committee was unable to settle the matter in three or four days, because many properties were involved. In the meantime, all of these properties were damaged and looted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to help the Chamber at all with restoration of these properties back to their rightful owners after the war?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I was already removed from the position of prime minister, but the ministry for the displaced and refugees was established, which worked along those lines, and the properties were returned, including flats. The community in general, and the international community, participated in funding the reconstructions of properties that were damaged. While those properties that were occupied by residents were in fact quite well-preserved and protected by those who occupied them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Religious sites in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I perhaps first ask a few clarifying questions on parts of the testimony which I might not fully understand. You said that there were Serbs who came to Banja Luka and evicted a Croat family and took them all the way over to Slavonia, to Okucani, in Croatia. You said you didn't know anything about this. "Only at the point when he realised in Gradiska that he was unable to get them across the border." Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't just one family that was evicted. Several families were evicted, several homes, and he took them over by bus. He was a Serb from Okucani, but I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if you say when he realised in Gradiska that he was unable to get them across the border, do I have to understand that the expedition failed to continue at the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was stopped in Gradiska, at the border, and then all of them were taken back to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's how many kilometres from Banja Luka, the border at Gradiska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe 58 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, did this happen in one day, then, or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it happened in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And nevertheless, they could not be returned to their homes because already Serbs from Okucani had been accommodated. So just for my understanding, that all happened in one day: They were evicted, and you said these were quite a number of families, and on that same day, Serbs were accommodated there in those flats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was my understanding. That's how I understood the person who told me so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you said you called the manager of the Bosna Hotel in order to accommodate the evicted Banja Luka citizens.
