Have you ever considered to call the Bosna Hotel manager to say that the Serbs should be accommodated in the Bosna Hotel rather than those who were evicted from their apartments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, because there were too many Serbs. There were about 70.000 Serb refugees in Banja Luka. And this was a smaller group of citizens who were evicted from their homes. And when I called the manager, he told me that he was able to accommodate them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that you did not understand my question. Let's take it that five or ten families were evicted from their flats. You said it was a bus full of people. Now, they returned to Banja Luka and find that on the same day their apartments had been occupied or were accommodating Serbs. Why didn't you call the Bosna Hotel manager and ask him to accommodate the persons who were occupying the apartments of those who were now returning from Gradiska to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Gradiska, yes, yes. Well, yes, those were the Croats from Banja Luka who were taken back from Gradiska because they were unable to cross the border. They were visited by the Red Cross and by the citizens of Banja Luka. It was them I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems that you still have not understood my question. Why did you not instruct this person who asked for your advice? Why didn't you say: Bring them back to their own apartments, and I'll call the Bosna manager to see whether the Serbs, who meanwhile occupy their apartments, that they were accommodated in the Bosna Hotel? Which would re-establish, I would say, the natural situation, that is, the Croats in their own apartments again and those who were in need of accommodation to be accommodated in the Bosna Hotel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were private homes, not apartment buildings that were involved --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The place where they lived, where these are apartments or private homes is not essential.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I asked that they be taken back to their homes. But he told me that they do not dare to. And I wanted to have them stop being afraid, and I thought that they would stop being afraid after several days staying at the hotel. However, I felt that I should not insist, that if I were to insist on this, while on the other hand I had several other thousand people who were driven away, Serbs driven from Slavonia, I felt that this was discrimination. The other Serbs would be opposed to this idea. And I would simply cause havoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you learned from the media that someone considered this very humanitarian gesture of yours as creating a camp in Hotel Bosna, which, from what I understand from your testimony, certainly was not the case, that you wanted to accommodate people against their will in Hotel Bosna. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then your testimony says that where the Executive Committee was willing to cover the cost for lodging and board, that you then, on the basis of this Croatian TV blaming you for turning Bosna Hotel into a camp, that you called the manager of the Bosna Hotel that he should immediately dissolve the camp. May I take it that the Croats couldn't stay any longer in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They could. They could have. But at their own expense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How long did they stay there at the expense of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not sure whether it was five or seven days, but it was a four-star hotel. We didn't have any other accommodation, because people did not want to go into collective accommodation if they had their own homes there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why didn't you say: It's a pure lie, what Croatian television tells us, so therefore, my decision that they should rather stay in the Bosna Hotel in order to get a safe feeling, rather than the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, we didn't have any difficulties bringing them back to their homes, because the tensions settled down. And it was of course too expensive for the municipality to cover these costs. We were able to do so, but only for that limited period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you said later on. What do I have to understand, later on? When did they return to their homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right after the municipality stopped covering their expenses at the hotel; Hotel Bosna, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, how did you get rid of those who were occupying these private homes, which were the reason why they could not return to their homes? I mean, how -- where did they go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Most of the Serbs who had come from Slavonia moved out to Serbia. So the majority were no longer in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But I'm talking about the specific group that occupied these five or ten homes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So just to try to better understand, and to summarise, and please correct me if I'm wrong: You said you were informed about an event which took place, as far as you're aware of, on the same day, that people were -- Croats were evicted from a number of homes in Banja Luka, taken to the border at Gradiska; upon return, could not go into their own homes again; then stayed in Hotel Bosna for a couple of days; and then, once you decided, on the basis of an untruthful television broadcast in Croatia, you decided not to pay any longer for the accommodation in the Hotel Bosna; and they all went home to their own homes again. Is that where the Serbs occupying these homes had, for reasons unknown, left again after one week? Is that a correct understanding of what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. However, I do not know what happened to the Serbs. I know that the HDZ representative in the Executive Committee kept visiting these Croats and took care of them, and he never gave me any indication that there had been any difficulties in them returning to their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us when this happened, approximately? Month, year.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the period of the fall of Slavonia, perhaps in May 1995 or 1994. But I believe it was in 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, it was not right from the beginning clear to me that we were hearing testimony on the 1995 events in this respect. But I may have overlooked something. I'm quite willing to accept that I have misinterpreted the testimony where I thought that it had -- that it took place in a time frame which we usually concentrate on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It may well be my fault for not having asked the witness that more specifically at an earlier stage. He gave that answer in relation to a fairly general question from me, it's fair to say, and he gave really the longest answer he'd given in the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, Mr. Josse, I think what happened is in the beginning of -- when you asked about the refugee problem, the witness started to tell us when it approximately started and then asked about when was the real summit of these refugee problems, he answered that it was in 1995. And then I think you took him back to the beginning. And it may have been a lack of concentration on my side that I did not notice when we moved back again to 1995. And I understood your questions taking the witness back from 1995 as being the most important -- well, where it was the high point of the refugee problem, taking him back, to take us back to -- well, of course, the period of time which is most relevant for this case, without saying that 1995 could never be relevant. And then we had a long story which was rather unclear to me, but now turns out to be somewhere in 1995. Well, it's at least good that matters have been clarified. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about an organisation called the SOS, please. What do you understand by those initials?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: This stands for Serbian Defence Forces, which spent a short period of time in Banja Luka, prior to the war, in early spring of 1992. I don't know who appointed them, who brought them to the municipality. I came to work in the morning and saw armed soldiers in uniform blocking the entrance to the municipality building. I was unable to enter the entrance for the staff. There were both the president and the vice-president of the municipality there. Vice-president, when he saw me there, he told me that Predrag Radic had appointed them. I went to Stojan Zupljanin, chief of the CSB, security services centre, to ask him what this was all about, what was this blockade of the municipality about. He asked his assistants how many armed policemen were there. He told them that there were 200 of them. The SOS forces stayed there for the day. The municipality did not work that day, not even the inspection service, which was duty-bound to work every day, was unable to do so. They were supposed to announce the number of those who died in the hospital every day, but they were unable to do it on that particular day. Later on, at the Assembly session, a request was read out by the SOS, the Serbian Defence Forces. As far as I can remember, there were nine requests, one of which was to launch an inquiry into the abuse of official power. An inquiry was in fact carried out, but nobody was found responsible for any abuse.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. It was the meeting of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What, if anything, did the SOS do in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: It was a paramilitary formation, or a parapolice formation; I'm not sure. Representatives of the international community who were present in Banja Luka invited us for a meeting, for a briefing in Hotel Bosna. There was Stojan Zupljanin, Predrag Radic, there was the president of the HDZ, Gabelic. There was Sajic, I, and Vukic, president of the SDS. I don't know whether there was anybody from the SDA. They claimed that they were able to protect Banja Luka from attacks with the help of the SOS. Gabelic told us that his son felt the presence of the SOS forces was stressful, that he lost his faculty of speech. I said that the district public prosecutor saw who these armed people were and went back home. He was unable to go to his workplace, because these were criminals. They could not have been there to protect the town. There were several of us who went to see General Talic, asking that he use his offices to dissolve the group. General Talic asked that we, members of the Assembly, see to it that the legalisation of this force is prevented. He wanted us to prevent this force from becoming legalised. So it happened that it was abolished, and SOS members were drafted into the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You described them as criminals. Why?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The district attorney said that. He said that some of them were prosecuted by him, that one of them had spent eight years in prison. I got that information from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you say they were criminals?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: They were paramilitaries. I personally didn't know a single one of them. However, we were afraid of them, me and other members of the Assembly, and we wanted the force to be disbanded. The MPs even wanted Knindze to come to Banja Luka in case a member of the SOS attacked one of the citizens. The Knindze were there for a few days. They wanted to be paid 100 German marks a day for their services. Ango Kograhovac [phoen], one of the directors of a local company, paid them that money. But in any case, that's how a possible conflict with the paramilitaries had been prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any criminal activities committed by the SOS whilst they were in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Women in the Municipal Assembly told us that some of them had taken jewellery from the local women when they were travelling on buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were the members of the SOS exclusively Serbs?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know any of them. I met one of them on the front line, and he was a Serb. He even said, which is totally unbelievable to me: Did we have to kill this man? But this is certainly not correct. He is somewhere in Germany, but he was a Serb, and I just met him by chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to say why Zupljanin was unable to control the SOS?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I can't say. He never told me anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the question assumed facts not precisely in evidence. I think we need a foundational question before that question is asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Was Zupljanin able to control the SOS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because the question suggests, as it was put initially, a fact which had not been established yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I accept the objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then first question is: Was Mr. Zupljanin able to control the SOS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was in charge of the police, and there were 3.000 police officers in Banja Luka. I don't know how many of them were on the front line. I suppose so. SOS was a very small group of armed people. It was not big.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certain sacred buildings within Banja Luka were destroyed during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let's deal in turn. Mosques. Are you able to say how many mosques were destroyed in Banja Luka during the war?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There were two big mosques, Ferhadija and Arnaudija, both under international protection. They were the two key mosques and they were destroyed. There were many small mosques, some of them wooden ones. I believe that there were 14 of them in the territory of Banja Luka. A majority of them were small ones, only there were two big ones. In the meantime, after the end of the war, quite a number of them have been restored, but the two big ones, the work has not even started on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you able to say when the two big mosques were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know the year. During the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sure I can lead on this. There is no doubt that they were deliberately destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There's no doubt about that. Radic was absolutely dissatisfied when these two mosques were destroyed. I was in his office at the time, and he was very angry. To this very day, it still isn't known who is responsible for the destruction of these two mosques.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any idea what efforts were made to find those who were responsible?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I am not in a position to do that. I was in the Executive Board of the municipality of Banja Luka, a member of the executive power, and it was the police and the judiciary who should have been responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask one clarifying question again, Mr. Josse. You several times referred to the police and the judiciary as being responsible for, well, investigating and adjudicating those who were responsible. Could you tell me: At what period of time are we talking about? I would say destruction of the mosques. I take it that if you say that the 14 -- most of the 14 were restored, that they first were at least damaged. The two great mosques and the 14 of which at least some have been damaged, when did this happen, approximately, in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were not damaged. They were razed to the ground. Arnaudija mosques and Ferhadija mosques. There was during the war, either in 1993 or 1994. I'm not sure of the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing of the kind happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the year. It was during the war, however. I don't think that they were destroyed in 1992. I believe that this happened somewhat later, in 1993 or 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you now talking about the two large mosques or about all 14, and the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about the two big ones that were in the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the 14 ones of which you said many of them were restored after the war, I understood this to be as a reference to earlier damage and perhaps even destruction. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did any of these destructions happen in 1992, or should I say damage or destructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know the year. I don't think that the destruction started in 1990. I believe it all started later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have some difficulties in following the interpreters, perhaps being not close enough to the microphone. Yes. Now, you said the police and the judiciary. Could you tell me, at the time you're referring to, what was the composition of the police? Had it changed since the beginning of the war? And I'm talking about composition in terms of ethnicity or nationality.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never received any information about that at the Executive Board meetings. In the leadership, the composition was changed, and since other ethnic groups that occupied those positions had left the town, only the Serbs remained. The police protect property and obtain information on the order of the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, you told us about the leadership. But on average, did you have no information at all on whether the police was still multi-ethnic in its lower regions or whether it had become more or less a mono-ethnic police force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never received that information, because the Ministry of the Interior is a body at the level of the Republic, and it is the minister who has to look after that. The municipality did not have any information about the police, no insight into it whatsoever, because the police is a body at the level of the Republic. Only from time to time did we review their reports on the security situation in Banja Luka, and that was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You had no idea about whether the composition, apart from what you told us already, that there were changes or considerable changes or whether it was still the same? I mean, I'm not asking about official reports, but just whether you knew.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know anything about that. There were a lot of police officers, and without an official report, I couldn't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You might have known some of the police officers, and you might have met them on the streets, to say: Well, I know that my neighbour from two streets from here is a police officer. I saw him frequently in the exercise of his police functions. I mean, sometimes you know things even without having received reports from the ministry. Could you tell us -- just give us an impression of what you experienced in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked in Jelsingrad, which is in the suburbs. I resided in the suburbs. I had very few occasions to see patrolmen. But I knew who their heads were. During the war, it was only the Serbs. I don't know who were police officers. I didn't know any of them personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to know the importance of the municipality of Banja Luka. How many people lived in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the 1991 census, 192.000. The town itself had 148.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse -- an early break -- not an early break, but at least a break that would give you some opportunity to -- could you tell us how much time you'd still need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. My estimate at 10 past 4.00 was about as bad as they can get.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We might have been responsible to some extent for that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Not really. I'm going to be questioning this witness until 7.00, almost certainly, now. So I'll take the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you find a suitable moment within the next ten minutes to have a break, then we'll have a break until close to 6.00 or 6.00, and then continue for another hour. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Catholic churches, were any of those destroyed in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Catholic church in the centre of town, one of the most beautiful in Banja Luka, is still standing. However, one in the suburbs, very close to my apartment, was destroyed during the war. I don't know about any of the others. The neighbourhood where that church was is called Petricevac. In the meantime, it has been restored. The Pope himself was present some two or three years ago for the consecration of that newly restored church.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If I may, I'll accept Your Honour's offer at this point in time, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then adjourn until five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, you may continue once the witness is there. Mr. Kasagic, Mr. Josse will continue his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Really, Mr. Kasagic, I'm going to ask you a series of what I hope are fairly specific questions in the next few minutes. The first is: You described the ethnic make-up of the Executive Committee in Banja Luka at the start of the war. Were there any non-Serbs who served on the Executive Committee during the war?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: There was a Croat from the HDZ. The others left Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The Croat from the HDZ, what was his name, please?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Anton Ruzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And what was his role on the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: He was the deputy president of the president of the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And for how long did he serve with you on the Executive Committee?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: From the moment the Executive Committee was elected until the moment I became the president of government. But even when I left, he remained serving on the Executive Committee.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Quite important translation point, Your Honour. You were prime minister, not president of the government, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Where I come from, it's one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just for purposes of linguistic clarification, this was an issue that was raised perhaps before Mr. Josse was part of the case, and that was the use of the term "government," not to mean the overall political authorities but to mean that specific body that is presided over by either the president of the government or the prime minister, depending on the term used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Being ministers together headed by the prime minister, but not including the Presidency of the Republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct. I think that's an issue that was -- and I don't mean to pre-empt the questions, but I think if the witness was trying to explain, and I think it's been addressed before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful. I apologise to the interpreter if I've done any injustice to her.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next matter, Mr. Kasagic, is this: Are you aware of an incident at the Kozara relay station, where, as a result of a transmitter being altered in some way, Sarajevo Television was no longer being received in Banja Luka and instead Belgrade Television was received?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I'm aware of that. I believe that this happened in late 1990. In Banja Luka, we could watch Sarajevo and Zagreb TV, but not Belgrade TV. When the nationalistic tensions started, one group of people went up and turned the transmitter to face Belgrade, and from then on we could follow the programmes from Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there any truth in the suggestion that you attended a party to celebrate this event at the Europa restaurant, at the bottom of the Kozara Mountain?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. I'm not even aware of the fact that there was such a celebration. And as for this hotel, or the restaurant Europa, I was there long before the war, when Jelsingrad celebrated 50 years of its existence, and never again after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there any truth, Mr. Kasagic, in the allegation that you carried out a plan to remove all non-Serb managers from all state-owned companies, such as the electric company?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. This was a decision, or rather, a conclusion of the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina. At the Assembly of AR Krajina, I asked for the conclusion to be abolished. This conclusion was published in the Official Gazette on issue number 5 of AR Krajina. I said at that assembly that one day we would be ashamed of that decision. However, only four of us voted against that decision and that decision remained in effect, in other words, this decision of the AR Krajina was never abolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to digress there for a moment. What was your view of the AR Krajina, your general view of it?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I advocated the position that it was an association of municipalities in line with the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it had its competencies along these lines, and the competency was in terms of commerce and in terms of defence. Yugoslavia was very much geared towards defence, and everybody was duty-bound to have its defence plans, companies and municipalities included. When the Crisis Staff came into existence and when they started passing some very ridiculous decisions, some at the expense of the Serbian people, I started to object those decisions. However, I didn't have much influence on these decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Going back to what I was asking you a few moments ago: Is there any truth in the suggestion that you were a leading force in the ethnic cleansing of all non-Serbs in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I heard that some people that evicted non-Serbs out of their houses evoked my name. I've already mentioned that. And I also told you how I asked for protection of people in their homes. However, I didn't have any say in that, and I heard that the Croats who had settled in Croatia said on Radio Gradiska that Rajko Kasagic was amongst the influential people in that respect. However, I never participated in any of that. I never cooperated with any in that. I never visited a single house. All to the contrary; I was never involved in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You've already dealt with this to some extent, but I should ask you again. What about the suggestion that you were involved in the resettlement of Serbs into vacated Muslim homes in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Not me personally, but the Executive Committee, they issued temporary certificates on temporary usage of those houses and apartments. I was the president of the Executive Committee and I was the one who signed those certificates or permits or decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you're aware, did you sign any eviction orders?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Certainly not. Absolutely not. There are minutes of the meetings of the Executive Committee dating to that period here, at The Hague Tribunal, and you can consult them to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the suggestion that you were involved in this ethnic cleansing and resettlement of Serbs with someone called FNU Denic, who was head of the municipal military department? Did you cooperate with him in these activities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Denic was in charge of defence, and he also was in charge of mobilisation of people for the front lines. Once I gave a statement in the public media talking about Denic who had engaged directors for mobilisation. My view was that directors should be in charge of the work of their companies. In my view, defence was something that was amongst the competencies of the Republic rather than of particular municipalities, and that is why I could not cooperate with him. He was in charge of defence and I worked in the municipality. I'm not even aware of the fact that he might have been doing something in that respect. I never heard any such thing. This is the first time I hear it, the first time I hear that he was involved in any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Finally, so far as this set of questions is concerned, what do you say to the suggestion that you, in conjunction with Mr. Zupljanin, became very wealthy from the illegal smuggling of fuel?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say a thing. The only thing I can say is that there were a lot of rumours in the war, a lot of lies. I heard stories about my company on Cyprus, in Athens, in London. I have two daughters in the States. I do not have a son, although some say that my son has a company somewhere. I never heard of Zupljanin smuggling oil, and especially doing it with me. People who spread those stories or believed in them realised after a while that I don't have any money, and they wondered how come I don't spend that money. And then they realised I don't have the money and then they started saying, Rajko is a fool. He didn't get anything for himself. And I am an intellectual. I have authored six books. I have become a full-time professor at the university, and that is enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think again to some extent you've answered the next question, but I want to ask it anyway. Are you very wealthy?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I've always said, and I will say again, that I'm wealthy in spirit. I have what I had before the war, and nothing new. A year ago I bought a new Skoda Fabia from the proceeds of my current job. I said publicly on TV to all the citizens that if any of them is aware of my assets abroad or any surplus on what I had before the war, I will willingly share that with them. I will give away anything that they think I have. I fear God. That is why I have never obtained anything illegally. I fear of God's punishment. The love of silver is punishable by God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you very much, Mr. Josse. Sorry for interrupting you. I'd like to ask a question of the witness. Going back to what you said on several occasions during your testimony, I noted that you make a clear distinction between things pertaining to local powers and things pertaining possibly to central powers. So at the level of the Republic or of the government. I'd like to know this: Were there any decisions taken, lato sensu, widely speaking, by the central government, a decision that you would have disapproved of, and if there were any, which were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember any such decisions that were contested by the Executive Committee. However, the Executive Committee proposed to the central government, i.e., to the government of Republika Srpska, that there should be more activities geared towards the rule of law. We proposed that administrative procedures should be carried out at two levels, and this wasn't done. So the Executive Board was the authority that issued decisions on appeal, because the central government failed to introduce a two-instance procedure in the administrative -- into the administrative proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am aware that you claim to be a legalist. I am not asking you whether local institutions challenged or whether local institutions suggested to the central government to do such things, this or that. But I'm asking you whether you, as a citizen, you were able to disagree with given decisions taken by the central powers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an MP, I intervened about that at the parliament session. I contested a few things, I agreed with some others, but I don't remember any details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... you challenged, which decisions you were against, and which you, in all conscience, could not agree with as a parliamentarian, as representative of your municipality or as a simple citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were many Assembly sessions. Many decisions were taken at every of them. At this moment, as I sit here, I can't remember anything specific, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Earlier on you mentioned the decision taken by the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. It was a plan aimed at evicting non-Serbs from a number of companies, or dismissing them, and you said that you were against it and that you opposed that decision. Where did you express your opposition, on what specific occasion did you do so, and how did you express your disagreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was an Assembly of AR Krajina in Banja Luka, in the culture hall currently known as Banski Dvor. I spoke publicly at that assembly, and I said that this decision should be voted for or against and that we would be ashamed of that decision. This was at the Assembly of AR Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that's where your protests ended. It was during a public session, so you did not send any communique, a release, a report, to people in positions of power, within the central powers that you might have known. That ended there. Right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's where it ended. This was no secret. Everybody knew that. The media were informed about what had happened and they informed the general public about that. But you have to bear in mind that this was the state of war and it was dangerous to act differently. I already had problems with the president of the Crisis Staff of AR Krajina and its president. At the assembly sessions, as MPs, we also entered into conflict with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This goes together with my next question. To what extent do you feel that you were a free citizen during the events? What was the capacity for you to oppose decisions? You said you were afraid, but who were you afraid of? What were you afraid of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Armed people. Everybody was armed. All the soldiers carried arms and brought it into Banja Luka. There was a lot of shooting, a lot of stray bullets which killed people. On one occasion, I spoke to General Talic, and I asked him not to allow soldiers to bring arms home but to leave them on the front line. During the war, I don't know when exactly this was, my house was fired at by a Zolja. On that night, I was not home. I was in Banja Luka. A projectile from Zolja hit the room where I was supposed to sleep. If I had been in my bed, I wouldn't be here today, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you afraid of the people working within the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a free person, a brave person. I was not afraid of entering into conflict with them if my way of thinking differed from theirs. I was not afraid at the moment when information came from the High Representative that I was supposed to be assassinated. I said to a journalist, a foreign journalist: If that is my lot, then I would be killed. And if that is not to be my lot, then the person who is supposed to assassinate me will be killed on the way to assassinate me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This assassination that you could fear could have come, could it, from the people on the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who could it come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was much later. I had already been removed from the position of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One very short question. Did the ARK Assembly have a general power to overrule all decisions from the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Assembly was duty-bound to either accept or reject conclusions or decisions issued by the Crisis Staff. The Crisis Staff was duty-bound to submit information on all the decisions and conclusions that had been taken before the next Assembly session. And the Assembly was in a position to either adopt those conclusions or decisions or reject them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember any occasion where they rejected decisions taken by the ARK Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was only once at that one session. I don't know whether there were any other sessions of the Assembly after that, as I did not attend any of them. In 1992, I did not attend the AR Krajina Assembly meeting. I went to the meeting of the parliament on Mount Jahorina. I did not consider this Assembly session to be any important [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, or did I misunderstand your testimony: Didn't you say that this decision to fire all non-Serb managers from the state-owned companies that -- I remember that you said only -- that you raised the matter and that only four votes were cast in favour of rejecting the decision. Was that the one session you were just talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the session, not the one in 1992 which I didn't attend, but the second one that I attended on purpose. I was at that Assembly session with the intent to propose the abolishment of such a decision issued by the Crisis Staff. I spoke publicly. I advocated the abolition of such decision, but this was not accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us who voted in favour of your proposal to abolish this decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know their names. One, as far as I remember, was from Gradiska, but I don't know his name. And the other two, I don't know their names. There were four of us in favour of my proposal. But I don't know any of the names. This man from Gradiska who opposed this decision, I never knew his name, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that that's all on the record of the ARK Assembly meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it should be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You understand, Mr. Josse, that especially to find objective support for such testimony, the Chamber, of course, would very much like to see it and to better understand what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I've already made a comment to my left to that effect, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You mentioned, in the course of the questions that Judge Hanoteau asked you, that you had your problems with the president of the Crisis Staff of the AR Krajina. And you clearly just told us about one of those problems. Are there any other problems that you are able to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I was on very friendly terms with a businessman, also from Banja Luka, who was a member of the government before me. He is a refugee from Zagreb who had a company which was involved in commerce and construction works. In the meantime, he passed away. His business was going on really well, and it was thought that we had some interests in our relationship, but we were merely good friends. It was, I felt, in our interest that the economy was operational, because that was our future. He being a civil engineer probably could not really grasp what the significance of the economy was and in what relation commerce stood to construction works. At these meetings, very often he spoke of some economic embezzlement, mentioning exactly that man, Rajko Vukovic, saying that one day the fact that he was involved in embezzlement was going to come to surface. However, none of that sort of information that would indicate any such embezzlements ever appeared in the public. The Municipal Assembly had authorised the Executive Committee shortly before the war to administer whatever the customs had seized in their warehouse in Banja Luka, or rather, the vehicles that were there. However, the Crisis Staff of AR Krajina decided that they should be the ones to use the vehicles, and the Executive Committee was only in the position to inform the Municipal Assembly that it had been denied its authority to decide about it, although I myself thought that it would have been highly improper of the Executive Committee to decide about these vehicles, which, after all, were the property of the Republican organs. Therefore, I was actually quite pleased that this was taken off our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, if I may, now to another topic. I want to ask you this: Do you recall attending any meetings of any sort at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: In 1991 I did not attend any meeting in Holiday Inn. As MPs of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we only spent the night in Holiday Inn. We stayed there at the expense of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd still invite you to have a look at this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The exhibit number you are presenting to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's tab -- Exhibit 65, tab 64. Or it's the other way around, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think most of us by now understand. We give it a name after the witness has had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, you've had a chance to read that document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When was the first time that you saw that document?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Here in The Hague, and it was yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It's commonly known, at least in this courtroom, as the Variant A and B document. Was that something that you were familiar with at all in late 1991, early 1992, in the course of your work or political activity?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I don't remember hearing of it. If I did, I forgot. It did not have any actual meaning in practice, at least as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next thing I want to ask you goes back to, in fact -- related to something you were being asked about by the learned Judges not that long ago. You were being asked about criticisms that you might have of the government, and you said that you can't remember whether in fact you -- what specific criticisms you had now with the benefit of hindsight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The first government, headed by Professor Djeric, did not introduce a two-instance procedure. After a while, I asked that the prime minister resign. However, this proposal was not even discussed. It was ignored. And then a couple of months later, I resigned for my own private reasons. I was dissatisfied, because I seemed not to have been able to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You resigned from what?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: From my position as prime minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But we're talking about 1996, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. No. I believe it was in 1992, or it could have been 1993. Subsequently, Lukic was elected prime minister. He was also a professor at the university.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. The transcript says that you resigned from your position as prime minister. You weren't prime minister in 1992, were you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No, no. No. It wasn't -- I wasn't referring to myself. In December 1995 I was appointed, and I stayed in my position until the 15th of May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you. You were talking about Mr. Djeric resigning, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In 1992, did you attend meetings of the Republika Srpska Assembly?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I attended all the Assembly sessions. I believed it was my duty to participate in the work of the Assembly. But I did not keep any records, although I did take part in the work of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Were you aware of any discussion, informally, amongst deputies, about crimes that were being committed in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Publicly, at the Assembly session, no such thing was discussed. However, from the Prijedor deputies, I learnt that there was a public camp in Prijedor - Keraterm, I believe it was called - and that was the information that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Anything else other than that discussion with the Prijedor deputies? Any other discussion with any deputies about crimes?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. I know that a deputy in Srebrenica was killed. Nobody knew who had killed him. That was still at the time when we were part of Yugoslavia, when Bosnia-Herzegovina was part of Yugoslavia. He got killed as he was returning from negotiations with SDA members.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So far as the information the Prijedor deputies gave to you, was that anything you discussed with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't -- four years ago, when an ICTY lawyer spoke to me in Banja Luka, he asked me whether I knew that Karadzic had called over the phone and criticised the people about these camps, and I said that I didn't know what or if anybody knew anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Whilst on the subject of SDS deputies: You gave some evidence earlier about the SDS Deputies Club when the Assembly was part of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly. I now want to ask you about the Deputies Club in the Republika Srpska Assembly. Firstly, who was the chairman of the SDS Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The chairman of the SDS Deputies Club was Professor Maksimovic. He was a professor at the Sarajevo University.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What influence did Mr. Krajisnik have on that Deputies Club?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Right at the beginning, I stated that these first multi-party elections yielded the first multi-party parliament, where the deputies were free for the first time to speak their minds. It was dangerous to become a member of an ethnic party at the time when the League of Communists was still in power, but nobody could influence them, could influence their thoughts and what they were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: A specific question: Are you able to tell us when in 1992 Mr. Krajisnik visited Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you which year that was, but I know that he occasionally came there with the president of Republika Srpska. I know that on his arrival he would always go to the church. I note that there was a lady who approached him and told him, "President, you should take care of us." It was at the time when deputies of different ethnicities came into conflict already. He smiled at her with equanimity and told her, "Don't be afraid. Everything will be fine." After that, we went to see Vladika and spent some time with him, the Orthodox priest.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Orthodox bishop, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have you any recollection of Mr. Krajisnik being at a meeting in Banja Luka on the 22nd of April, 1992, along with General Talic, a meeting that was televised?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, really, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is the 22nd of April a significant day in the calendar of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I believe that there was a date in April which marked the day of liberation of Banja Luka in 1945, in World War II. This was a date that was celebrated in the period up to this recent war in Banja Luka. I believe that was the date, although I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But that doesn't help jog your memory about this meeting one way or the other; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. I did not attend the meeting because I'm sure I would remember it, had I been there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The notion of an extended Presidency within the Republika Srpska meant what to you?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: It meant to me something that was normal in the former Yugoslavia in the single-party system. There was always the most senior official, who would ask of the subordinate officials of the League of Communists and trade-unionists to be his -- for him to be their advisor, that he would give them some information and then they would pass them on. And in that context, you would have the Extended Presidency and not as in a decision-taking body. Because other organs, such as the parliament and the government, would continue discharging their functions as usual.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear -- as far as you were concerned, was Mr. Krajisnik a member of the Extended Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Even if it was mentioned, nobody paid any attention to it as an advisory body. Had it been a body taking decisions, then the Assembly would be there to confirm these decisions. But I don't recall ever there being any such decisions forwarded to the Assembly for either confirmation, adoption, or rejection. I believe that under the constitution, this body becomes active in the event of a declared state of war. It does not become active so long as all the other bodies are able to function as per normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When, if at all, was a state of war declared?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Republika Srpska never declared a state of war, but rather a state of -- an imminent threat of war. Although officers frequently asked that a state of war be declared, the parliament never did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me put this another way. Did you ever hear of any suggestion that Mr. Krajisnik was a member of the Extended Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: If I heard anything to that effect, I forgot about it, because this body was not important in terms of any decision-making. Had it been important as a decision-making body, I'm sure that as a deputy, I would have been aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to another topic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, in 1992, what was Mr. Krajisnik's role within the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was Speaker of the Parliament, and he was exceptionally good in chairing the parliament. We were all very satisfied with him. He did not abuse his position as the chairman, or the Speaker. He made it possible for everyone to speak their minds and present their views. I saw him as a person inclined towards democracy, which wasn't the case before, because of the single-party system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a president of an Executive Committee of a municipality and as a member of the Assembly, are you able to assess what control, if any, Mr. Krajisnik had over municipalities?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: He had none. He wasn't able to have any. Because all the deputies would have opposed such control. After all, they all originated from one municipality or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: As a member of the Republika Srpska Assembly, are you able to assess what control Mr. Krajisnik had over the police, either centrally or regionally, within the Republic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: Whether he was able to, and to what extent, cooperate with the chief of police, I don't know, but he could, of course, interact with minister of the interior. But he did not have any authority or competence over the police, nor did I ever hear of him exerting any pressure on the police, in any sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same question in relation to the army, please.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: One was unable to influence the military. They had their supreme command in Belgrade. They were generals of the Yugoslav People's Army. Those were professional soldiers who themselves stated that they had never been trained or taught anything about the civil war and didn't know much about it. Mr. Krajisnik was unable to influence them. Although parliamentarians sometimes discussed military matters and deputies used to call the military personnel communists.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about when the VRS was established? Did the situation change? Did Mr. Krajisnik then gain some control over the army?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: No. As a deputy, he was unable to have any control over the army. It was only the supreme commander of the armed forces and the military command who were able to have control. What their links with the supreme command in Belgrade were, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The same question in relation to the judiciary. What was his position in relation to them, please?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: The judiciary was autonomous, and thank God it was so. It was not active enough during the war because of the general dangers. Not everything functioned the way it should have. It was very difficult. There were criminal offences committed on the front line, and in the hinterland. But the judiciary, although limited by the state of an imminent threat of war, continued functioning quite well, and autonomously. The parliament elected judges and the president, Speaker of the Parliament, did not have any influence over that. The judges of Republika Srpska were elected by the parliament in Banja Luka. I don't know which year that was, but all the information related to that was sent to the deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Flowing from that, did Mr. Krajisnik have any power to punish individuals or groups within the Republic?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KASAGIC
utterances.text: He did not have any power to do so, and I don't know whether he did punish anyone. Whenever a person would come up with some criticism, then he would always agree, affirm that it was so. When the next person would raise another matter of criticism, then he would again affirm that. But as for punishing someone, I don't believe he did, and I don't think he would be able to find anyone who would disprove what I'm saying. He was not -- he did not have the authority to punish anyone under any regulations. I don't even know if he was able to deny someone to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to say I've timed that rather well. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No further questions. Before we finish, I would have one question related to one of your last questions, Mr. Josse. You said: "Thank God the judiciary was independent and the judiciary was functioning well." Did you ever hear of judges provisionally releasing those who were suspected to have committed serious crimes and then to be sent to the front line rather than to remain in gaol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not hear anything of the sort in connection with the judiciary. But I was once with minister of judiciary, Jovo Rosic, I believe it was at the time, in a prison, when one of the prisoners asked to be released in order to go to the front line. I don't know what they decided about this subsequently. I never spoke to him again. I said: Thank God, of course within the limits of their power, because war is an evil thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The last part of your answer suggests that it never happened. Is that what you want to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that I don't know whether this happened or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that answer. We have to finish for today. Let me just -- perhaps it's good that the witness is there. Mr. Tieger, you wanted to delay cross-examination until Friday; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That means, Mr. Josse, that you would call your next witness for examination-in-chief tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Two things on that. First of all, when I had the opportunity, I explained the position to Mr. Kasagic. He understands that he's unlikely to be required tomorrow. Secondly, to the best of our knowledge, our next witness is now in the air, on his way to this country, though I just hope that information is accurate. He certainly won't have landed here as of this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Nevertheless, tomorrow, in the afternoon, you would start the examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I think I've got no option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then there's -- from what we just discussed, Mr. Kasagic, we will continue tomorrow not with your cross-examination. Most likely it will start on Friday. Of course, it depends on what happens tomorrow in the afternoon. But so we'd like you to follow the guidance of the Victims and Witnesses Section, which will tell you whether or not your cross-examination will start on the basis of the information they will receive tomorrow, but you should make yourself available by next Friday. That would be in the -- yes, it would be in the afternoon as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is that -- I see the registrar nodding his head in agreement. I thought it was the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, it's in the morning. I made a mistake. I apologise for that. So we'd like you to keep yourself available for Friday morning. I also would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given until now and the testimony you are about to give in cross-examination, perhaps re-examination. Madam Usher, could I ask you to escort Mr. Kasagic out of the courtroom, because I've one or two other matters to briefly announce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one is, Mr. Josse, the Defence has asked whether we could sit on Tuesday, the 22nd of November, in the afternoon rather than in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I have to say, could I just make this observation: That rather presupposes that, and he may be in a position now to help us, that my learned friend is going to take most of Friday with this witness, and whoever is going to cross-examine Mr. Banduka is going to take most of Monday, the idea being that we will have that much more time to prepare the witness for whom we're going to make the protected application. So I should make it clear to the Court that I have some concerns that we have some short days coming up. I think Mr. Banduka will take most of tomorrow, as I've already indicated. So I don't think tomorrow will be a short day, but it's the two days thereafter that I'm concerned about, bearing in mind they're effectively cross-examination of each witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask Mr. Tieger. He might have an idea already on how much time cross-examination would take.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not a particularly refined or good one at this point, Your Honour. I -- based on previous experience, I think it's -- we'd probably fall at or close to the guideline. But no, I can't profess to have -- to be of great assistance to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The guideline would be close to anything between two and a half until three-quarters of an hour, 60 per cent of time in chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I say that primarily because we've always aimed toward that and we will continue to do so and that seems to have been what has transpired. But I really can't say on the basis of any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But whatever is the case, Mr. Josse, if it all would turn out that you would have to start earlier, then of course it wouldn't make that much of a difference whether we would be sitting in the morning or in the afternoon of next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, just this: That what I would endeavour to arrange is that the protected witness, or the proposed protected witness, come with me to the UNDU on Tuesday morning. That would be far more preferable than Monday afternoon, for the reasons that Your Honour knows about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore I take it that you have a keen interest in not starting any earlier than Tuesday, and preferably in the afternoon. So I now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. That remains our position. I just thought I should lay my cards on the table about -- I have some concerns about time going astray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I do understand that. But at least that would require scheduling and organisation for Tuesday in the afternoon, which has been arranged by now.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that brings me to the other matter you just raised, which is perhaps not a matter to be discussed in detail in open session. But you said that -- you were talking about a protected witness, whereas the Chamber has not received any request for protective measures until now, neither on the form of protection nor on the grounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That is correct. Nothing has been filed as of yet. We are working on it. I will see Mr. Stewart shortly. He was dealing with it, I know, early this morning. We needed to speak to the witness again for some further details. I'm aware of the urgency of the situation, as is he.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, especially when it is already considered to apply for protective measures, then of course the Chamber would like to receive requests as early as possible. And at the same time, the Chamber understands that sometimes even the party calling the witness may be surprised by a sudden wish for protective measures, and of course under those circumstances, we have to some extent accept that the request will be filed rather late or submitted rather late. Any other procedural matter? Because we've stolen already ten minutes of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour, just so members of our team can liaise with the victims and witness service tomorrow. Is Your Honour saying that if Mr. Banduka does not arrive here for some reason, Mr. Kasagic needs to be ready to resume his evidence at 2.15 tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course I said this to be available on Friday morning at the moment where I had no clear idea yet. Because the Chamber wants to avoid to sit on many short days, leaving only a couple of hours, one hour remaining on that day. Of course, we'd very much like to concentrate, and if the examination-in-chief -- the cross-examination would start tomorrow -- no. I asked Mr. Tieger whether he was ready and he said he's not. So therefore, I think it remains as it was before, that if we would finish early tomorrow -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I would have thought that the Prosecution could begin cross-examining Mr. Banduka, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Cross-examining Mr. Banduka. He'll be here anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Assuming Mr. Banduka is here, if he finishes before 7.00, then I would submit the Prosecution could begin cross-examining him. In effect, they've had two or three days longer to prepare for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. Of course, it depends a bit. If it would be 20 minutes, it might be splitting up the cross-examination to an extent which would not much assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if Mr. Banduka would not take that much time tomorrow in the afternoon, would you be ready or would counsel present be ready to start cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I actually am not in a position to answer that precisely. The issue is not simply the amount of time the individual lawyer has to get ready, but in distributing the tasks to other resources, limited resources, in a manner consistent with the schedule. Whether or not that presents any problem, I don't know. I can check with Mr. Harmon immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not wait any longer at this moment. If you would not be in a position to start cross-examination tomorrow, if there's some time left, would you please inform us by tomorrow morning so that we can take that into account, and a copy to Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Josse, this deals with the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And if for some reason Mr. Banduka is not here in the next few hours -- I mean, I hope to see him this evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then tomorrow morning we get a lot of e-mail messages from both parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Exactly. I will let everyone know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Communication is an essential part of conducting a trial. I again apologise to the technical staff and interpreters for this late finish. We'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.14 p.m.,
